raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old male, a computer engineer by profession, was found drowsy at home and was referred to a nearby medical center. There was history of a recent business trip to Greece which took almost 6 weeks. He was suffering from headache and fever and was drowsy when admitted in the hospital [modified Rankin scale (MRS) =2]. Preliminary workups were all negative and brain computed tomography scan (CTS) showed a small left frontal opercular intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) accompanied with mild hydrocephalus [Figure 1]. He refused to stay in the hospital for further investigations after improvement of his mental state. Headache, fever, and intermittent changes in his state of consciousness recurred after a month and he was admitted in our center after another attack of severe headache. At the time of admission, he was stuporous with mild right hemiparesis and pure motor dysphasia (MRS = 4). Brain CTS showed a left frontal opercular ICH [Figure 2]. Four-vessel digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed a left distal middle cerebral artery (MCA) aneurysm that was 12 x 9 mm in diameter and without an identifiable neck [Figure 3]. This aneurysm was visible in both anteroposterior (AP) and lateral views even though there were two other ill-defined aneurysm blebs only seen in the lateral view of the angiogram. These two blebs were located along the more proximal branches of M3 segment of left MCA [Figure 4].
Considering the past history of fever, headache, detectable neck rigidity, and ICH, the first impression was rupture of a mycotic aneurysm. None of the aneurysms had well-identifiable neck in the angiogram. It was planned to treat the presumable mycotic lesions with a trial of wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy including Vancomycin 1 g twice/day + Rifampin 600 mg three times/day and Tazocin 4.5 g three times/day. All of the preclinical studies were negative except for the following: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) =28, C-reactive protein (CRP) =3 plus, and positive serology for brucellosis (direct Coomb's test/Brucella micro agglutination test) both in his plasma and CSF with the agglutinin titer of 1/160 and 1/80, respectively. CSF analysis was compatible with partially treated meningitis: WBC = 500/mm3, polymorphoneuclears 60%, lymphocytes = 40%, protein = 55.3mg/dl, and sugar = 56 mg/dl.
His general condition improved moderately after 3 weeks of antibiotic therapy (MRS 3), but intermittent fever persisted and the CSF picture did not change notably. A brain computed tomographic angiography (CTA) did not show any regression in the size of the distal MCA aneurysm. The other two ill-defined aneurysms noted in the previous DSA were well elucidated in the new CTA [Figure 5].
Considering the available facilities, it was decided to treat the aneurysms surgically and it was planned for either clipping-only or excision with reconstruction bypass surgery of the aneurysms according to the findings during surgery. A left posterior temporoparietal craniotomy was done after 30 days of antibiotic therapy. The dura was opened, taking care of the arachnoidal adhesions visible beneath the dura, and attached to one of the cortically exposed aneurysms. A small aneurysm was located along one of the cortical branches of M4, along the superior temporal gyrus with adhesions in the surrounding subarachnoid space. The arachnoid could be dissected sharply. The aneurysm was a small one located on a distal M4 branch, without a clippable neck. It was coagulated and excised. The second aneurysm was located along M3 segment of the frontal branch of MCA. It was dissected, clipped, and resected. The clip could be removed after micro-coagulation of the parent artery [Figure 6a and b]. The more distal dissection of Sylvian fissure revealed a third small aneurysm located more distally along the M4 segment of MCA, which was dissected, clipped, coagulated, and excised. The histopathological examination of the resected aneurysms was compatible with "mycotic aneurysm" [Figure 7a-c].
The patient's postoperative course was uneventful. Considering the positive serology for brucellosis both in plasma and CSF, the anti-brucella antibiotic regimen was continued. The patient could be discharged after 1 month with improvement of fever and stuttering (MRS 2). The anti-brucella medications were continued for another 6 weeks and negative serology tests achieved. The postoperative CTA performed after 1 year confirmed no aneurysmal dilatation along the course of MCA [Figure 8].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male computer engineer presented with acute severe headache, fever, stupor, right hemiparesis, and pure motor dysphasia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever, headache, and drowsiness (MRS = 2) following a 6-week business trip to Greece. Initial brain CT showed a small left frontal opercular intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), and mild hydrocephalus. He left against medical advice upon transient mental improvement. One month later, severe headache, fever, and altered consciousness recurred. Upon readmission, he was stuporous with mild right hemiparesis and pure motor dysphasia (MRS = 4).
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: computer engineer. Travel history: 6-week business trip to Greece shortly before symptom onset. Prior medical illnesses, medications, and dairy/animal exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe headache, fever, fluctuating consciousness, right-sided weakness, motor speech difficulty. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Stuporous mental state (MRS = 4), neck rigidity, mild right hemiparesis, pure motor dysphasia. Febrile with intermittent fever spikes. General condition improved to MRS = 3 after 3 weeks of antibiotics, and discharged at MRS = 2.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial brain CT scan: small left frontal opercular ICH, IVH, and mild hydrocephalus; readmission CT confirmed left frontal opercular ICH. Laboratory workup: ESR 28 mm/h, CRP 3+; preclinical workup otherwise negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: WBC 500/mm^3 (60% polymorphonuclears, 40% lymphocytes), protein 55.3 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL (compatible with partially treated meningitis). 4-vessel digital subtraction angiography (DSA): left distal middle cerebral artery (MCA) aneurysm measuring 12 x 9 mm without an identifiable neck, plus two ill-defined aneurysm blebs on proximal M3 branches of left MCA. Brain CT angiography (CTA) at 3 weeks: persistent distal MCA aneurysm and well-visualized M3 aneurysms without regression. Neurosurgical operation: left posterior temporoparietal craniotomy, micro-dissection of sylvian fissure and arachnoid adhesions, clipping and excision/coagulation of 3 mycotic aneurysms on M3 and M4 branches. Histopathology: compatible with mycotic aneurysms. Follow-up 1-year CTA: no residual aneurysmal dilatation along the MCA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis complicated by multiple intracranial infectious (mycotic) middle cerebral artery aneurysms, meningitis, and intracerebral/intraventricular hemorrhage.
Confirmation: Direct Coombs test / Brucella microagglutination test positive in plasma (titer 1/160) and in CSF (titer 1/80); histopathology of resected aneurysms confirmed mycotic aneurysms.
Differentials ruled out: Non-infectious intracranial aneurysms / arteriovenous malformations ruled out by angiography, serology, and histopathology.
Treatment & Outcome: Empirical vancomycin (1 g BID), rifampin (600 mg TID), and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g TID) administered for 30 days prior to craniotomy, followed by surgical clipping and excision of all 3 mycotic aneurysms; targeted anti-brucella antibiotic therapy continued postoperatively for 10 weeks total until negative serologies were achieved. The patient achieved excellent neurological recovery (MRS = 2) with resolved stuttering, afebrile state, and normal 1-year follow-up CTA.
